preamble: Loss of laterality in Arabic ḍād ⟨ض⟩: the emphatic lateral of Classical Arabic, usually reconstructed as pharyngealized [ɮˤ] (or an affricate [dɮˤ]), ends up as the emphatic stop [dˤ] of Modern Standard Arabic and of Egyptian and Levantine Arabic, but indirectly: in speech ɮˤ first merged with ẓāʾ [ðˤ], which became [dˤ] only in dialects that turned dental fricatives into stops; many dialects (most of Arabia, Iraq, Tunisia) keep [ðˤ]. Sibawayh described ḍād as articulated between the side of the tongue and the molars, and old loans keep a lateral: Spanish alcalde < al-qāḍī 'the judge', albayalde < bayāḍ 'white lead', arrabal and Old Leonese arraualde < rabaḍ 'suburb', Hausa alƙali, Akkadian ld or lṭ. Modern South Arabian cognates still have a lateral where Arabic has dˤ. Further back, the sound goes back to Proto-Semitic *ṣ́, reconstructed as an ejective lateral [ɬʼ] that survives in Modern South Arabian. In the reading tradition, Qur'an readers later assigned [dˤ] to ḍād to keep it apart from ẓāʾ (Wiktionary, ض), so the Modern Standard Arabic value is partly a learned reassignment rather than a single natural change. The source is pharyngealized [ɮˤ], approximated here by plain [ɮ] (the same change is also filed from [ɮˤ]), and André Roman proposed [ʑˤ] instead, so the exact starting value is debated.
